The TROTSKY I ended up with, largely with crosses, is a good attempt at writing the name down in English so that the pronunciation quite closely matches the Slavic original. As a kid I read the Catwings books by Ursula K. Le Guin. They absolutely captured my imagination.

I only now noticed the column photo. I did a cartoonish double take - that's Warsaw! In spring ducklings hatch in the decorative pools of the Łazienki Królewskie park. The mother ducks then lead their chicks to the nearby Wisła (Vistula) river. The problem is, between the park and the river there is one of Warsaw's most important thoroughfares, Wisłostrada. The city organizes a whole system of protecting the ducks - Straż Miejska (City Guard, municipal police) and an army of volunteers stand watch throughout the day for weeks, and they stop traffic whenever a family of ducks want to cross the street - 6 lanes of traffic are halted, and these super cute, little birds waddle across the asphalt. I took a lpost-solve look at MARE’S NEST, because while I’ve heard the phrase before, it’s not a phrase I’ve ever used.  It has two disparate meanings.

The more widespread meaning is how it’s clued today – a confused mess.  

But I also like its original meaning: a false discovery, where someone has found something remarkable, then it turns out to be worthless.  That is, a misconception.  This meaning makes sense, because mares don’t build nests.  Two classic example are the Martian Canals and the Piltdown Man.

Everyday examples include the belief that “premium” fuel will improve the performance of a standard economy vehicle, and the belief that we only use 10% of our brains.

Buy 2 bags of cranberries as soon as they appear in the grocery store--usually well ahead of holiday cookery.  Pick them over with care and discard those with blemishes or spoilage.  Rinse well.  These can be frozen without harm to results.  Since the bags Measure out 1 lb; the remainder can be used for cranberry-orange relish.  You will want a half-dozen nice oranges; grate some rind and  juice about 4 or 5 for 1 cup fresh OJ.  In a deep pan, combine OJ, 1/2 cup water, 1 1/2 cups sugar, and the berries.  Bring to a boil and cook quickly until the berries have popped and softened; some will remain whole.  Cooking will take about 6 minutes BUT cook for 15 if you want sauce to be more 'jellied.' Stir in the grated orange rind.  Of course you know to have sterilized jars, lids, etc.  No need to refrigerate.
